citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [patient care practices and the hospital environment may facilitate the transmission of microorganisms among patients. The selective pressure of intense antibiotic use promotes antibiotic resistance.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: What constitutes 'Standard Precautions' in a healthcare environment?
back: Routine care for all patients to limit contact with: 1. Secretions and biological fluids. 2. Skin lesions. 3. Mucous membranes. 4. Blood.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions should be applied to the care of all patients. This includes limiting health care worker contact with all secretions or biological fluids; skin lesions, mucous membranes, and blood or body fluids.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: How does interruption of transmission effectively control healthcare-associated infections?
back: It changes environmental factors (e.g., hand-washing, water treatment) to prevent infective agents from entering a susceptible host's body.
citation: Page 127 (Book Page): [interruption of transmission... may mean changing some components of man's environment to prevent the infective agent... from entering the body of susceptible person.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Isolation' and 'Quarantine' in infection control.
back: 1. Isolation: Separation of known infected persons during communicability. 2. Quarantine: Limitation of movement for healthy persons exposed during the incubation period.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page)/127: [Isolation is defined as 'separation... of infected persons... from others'. Quarantine applies to restrictions on the healthy contacts of an infectious disease.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: A patient develops purulent discharge at a surgical site 14 days post-op. What is the immediate isolation priority?
back: The patient must be physically isolated (Barrier Nursing) to prevent direct/indirect transfer of the infectious agent to other susceptible hosts.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page)/366: [Infectious patients must be isolated... The purpose of isolation is to protect the community by preventing transfer of infection from the reservoir to the possible susceptible hosts.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: Which method is used to sterilize heat-sensitive surgical instruments like endoscopes?
back: Ethylene oxide gas. It achieves sterilization by alkylating essential proteins and nucleic acids in microorganisms.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: What are the simplified clinical criteria for diagnosing Nosocomial (Hospital-Acquired) Pneumonia?
back: Respiratory symptoms with ≥2 signs during hospital stay: 1. Purulent sputum. 2. New infiltrate on chest radiograph.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Table 1: Respiratory symptoms with at least two of the following signs appearing during hospitalization: purulent sputum, new infiltrate on chest radiograph.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: Why is hand hygiene the most vital component of transmission-based precautions?
back: Hands are the primary vector for transmission. Thorough washing or alcohol-based disinfection breaks the most common direct contact route for HAIs.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: Distinguish Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) from Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) based on hospital stay.
back: HAP presents ≥48 hours after admission and was not incubating upon entry. CAP presents <48 hours after admission.
citation: Page 560 (Book Page): [Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined as an episode of pneumonia that presents at least 48 hours after admission to hospital and was not incubating at the time of admission.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: What is the primary objective of using a 'Surgical Safety Checklist'?
back: To standardize surgical processes and reduce errors (e.g., wrong site, retained swabs) through team-based situational awareness at three critical time points.
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [The benefits of standardisation of surgical processes... the checklist, which, when properly implemented, has been shown to improve surgical outcomes.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Q: State the standard autoclave parameters for the sterilization of surgical equipment.
back: Steam exposure at 121°C under 15 lb/in² pressure for 15–20 minutes to kill highly resistant bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page)/233: [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving... steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Define the three core components of Standard Precautions used for all hospital patients.
back: 1. Hand hygiene. 2. Personal Protective Equipment (gloves, gowns, masks). 3. Safe sharps and waste disposal.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): Standard precautions should be applied to the care of all patients. This includes... gloves, gown, mask and eye protection... All sharps should be handled with extreme care.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Explain how adherence to hand hygiene reduces the transmission of Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAIs).
back: It removes transient pathogenic flora from the hands of staff, blocking the most common route of cross-infection between patients and the hospital environment.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Contrast the clinical purpose of 'Isolation' versus 'Quarantine' in infection control.
back: - Isolation: Separation of infected persons during the period of communicability. - Quarantine: Limitation of movement of healthy persons exposed to infection for the incubation period.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): Isolation is defined as 'separation, for the period of communicability of infected persons'. Page 127 (Book Page): In contrast to isolation, quarantine applies to restrictions on the healthy contacts.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: A post-operative patient develops cellulitis at the surgical site. Which specific adherence breach does this represent?
back: Failure in surgical site precautions, typically involving poor aseptic technique, contaminated operating environments, or inadequate preoperative skin preparation.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: What is the pharmacologically optimal timing for antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent surgical site infections?
back: Administration within 60 minutes before the skin incision to ensure peak therapeutic tissue concentrations at the time of potential contamination.
citation: Page 241 (Book Page): Has antibiotic prophylaxis been given within the last 60 minutes?

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: State the temporal diagnostic criteria used to define an infection as nosocomial/hospital-acquired.
back: An infection acquired during hospital care that was not present or incubating at admission, typically occurring more than 48 hours after admission.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): Nosocomial infections... are infections acquired during hospital care which are not present or incubating at admission. Infections occurring more than 48 hours after admission are usually considered nosocomial.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Apply transmission-based precautions to effectively reduce the incidence of Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP).
back: Implement aseptic intubation/suctioning, use sterile water for oxygen therapy, and limit the duration of mechanical ventilation to break the transmission chain.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): Pneumonia Ventilator-associated: Aseptic intubation and suctioning; Limit duration... Sterile water for oxygen and aerosol therapy.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Differentiate the isolation requirements for Pulmonary Tuberculosis versus Cholera based on their transmission routes.
back: - TB: Airborne/Droplet precautions (isolated until 3 weeks of chemotherapy). - Cholera: Contact/Enteric precautions (isolated for 3 days after starting tetracyclines).
citation: Page 127 (Book Page): Table 41: Cholera: 3 days after tetracyclines started... Tuberculosis: Until 3 weeks of effective chemotherapy.

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Describe the three-part epidemiological cycle involved in the transmission of infectious diseases.
back: 1. The reservoir or source of infection. 2. The route(s) of transmission. 3. The susceptible host (people at risk).
citation: Page 125 (Book Page): Broadly these are measures... 1. The reservoir or source of infection 2. The route(s) of transmission 3. The susceptible host (people at risk).

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: What is the primary biochemical mechanism by which 70% ethanol acts as a skin antiseptic?
back: It disorganizes the lipid structure in cell membranes and denatures microbial proteins; water is required for maximal biocidal activity.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): It acts mainly by disorganizing the lipid structure in membranes, but it denatures proteins as well. Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the fundamental difference between sterilization and disinfection?
back:
- Sterilization: Killing/removal of ALL microorganisms including spores.
- Disinfection: Killing of many microorganisms/pathogens; bacterial spores often survive.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism by which heat kills microorganisms during sterilization?
back:
- Primarily denatures proteins.
- Secondary: Membrane damage and enzymatic cleavage of DNA.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [In general, heat kills by denaturing proteins, but membrane damage and enzymatic cleavage of DNA may also be involved.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Contrast the clinical application of disinfectants versus antiseptics.
back:
- Disinfectants: Stronger/corrosive; used for inanimate objects (fomites).
- Antiseptics: Less toxic; safe for skin and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Disinfectants vary... from the corrosive phenol-containing compounds, which should be used only on inanimate objects, to less toxic materials such as ethanol and iodine, which can be used on skin surfaces... called antiseptics.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which sterilization method is mandated for heat-sensitive surgical plastics and why?
back:
- Method: Ethylene oxide gas.
- Reason: Alkylates proteins and nucleic acids without heat damage to materials.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics. It kills by alkylating both proteins and nucleic acids.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol more effective as an antiseptic than 100% ethanol?
back: - Maximal activity requires the presence of water to facilitate protein denaturation and membrane disruption.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What are the standard parameters for effective sterilization via autoclaving?
back:
- Temperature: 121°C.
- Pressure: 15 lb/in².
- Time: 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [an autoclave chamber is used in which steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Explain why filtration is used to prepare intravenous solutions for medical use.
back:
- Removes heat-sensitive components and bacterial spores.
- Ensures solutions are pyrogen-free by removing heat-resistant endotoxins from gram-negative cell walls.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [Filtration is the preferred method of sterilizing... solutions for intravenous use were autoclaved, but heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls... caused fever... solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which agent is clinically superior for skin prep before drawing a blood culture and why?
back:
- Iodine-containing compounds (Tincture of iodine).
- Reason: More effective than alcohol against common skin flora like Staphylococcus epidermidis.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Iodine is the most effective skin antiseptic used in medical practice and should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture... contamination with skin flora such as Staphylococcus epidermidis can be a problem.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: How does pasteurization differ from sterilization in its effect on milk-borne pathogens?
back:
- Kills vegetative cells of pathogens (Mycobacterium bovis, Salmonella).
- Does NOT achieve sterilization as spores and some organisms survive.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [Pasteurization... is sufficient to kill the vegetative cells of the milk-borne pathogens... but not to sterilize the milk.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which biological indicator is used to confirm the efficacy of an autoclave cycle?
back: - Spore-forming organisms (e.g., Clostridium or Geobacillus stearothermophilus) due to their extreme heat resistance.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [To test the effectiveness of the autoclaving process, spore-forming organisms, such as members of the genus Clostridium, are used.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Define sterilization in terms of its effect on microbial life.
back: The absolute killing or removal of all microorganisms, including highly resistant bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, which are highly resistant.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is moist heat (autoclaving) more effective than dry heat for sterilization?
back: Water aids in disrupting noncovalent bonds (hydrogen bonds) that hold protein chains together in secondary and tertiary structures.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [Moist heat sterilizes at a lower temperature than dry heat, because water aids in the disruption of noncovalent bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds), which hold protein chains together.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the defining difference between disinfection and sterilization regarding spores?
back: Sterilization kills all spores; disinfection kills most pathogens but allows some bacterial spores to survive.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which method is preferred for sterilizing heat-sensitive respiratory therapy equipment or endoscopes?
back: Glutaraldehyde (2% solution) or Ethylene oxide gas.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [In hospitals, [glutaraldehyde] is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes, and hemodialysis equipment.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of action for 70% ethanol used in skin antisepsis?
back: Disorganization of lipid structures in cell membranes and denaturation of proteins.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [It acts mainly by disorganizing the lipid structure in membranes, but it denatures proteins as well.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: State the standard temperature, pressure, and time parameters for effective autoclaving.
back: 121°C at 15 lb/in² pressure for 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in² for 15 minutes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why must intravenous solutions be filtered to become 'pyrogen-free' despite subsequent autoclaving?
back: To remove heat-resistant endotoxins from dead gram-negative bacteria that cause fever in recipients.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls of the dead gram-negative bacteria caused fever in recipients of the solutions. Therefore, solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free prior to autoclaving.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Distinguish between an 'antiseptic' and a 'disinfectant' based on the site of application.
back: Antiseptics: Used on living tissue (skin/mucosa). Disinfectants: Used on inanimate objects/surfaces.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is pasteurization considered disinfection rather than sterilization?
back: It kills vegetative cells of milk-borne pathogens (e.g., Salmonella, Brucella) but does not destroy all organisms or spores.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [This is sufficient to kill the vegetative cells of the milk-borne pathogens... but not to sterilize the milk.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which specific gas is used to sterilize heat-sensitive surgical plastics and instruments?
back: Ethylene oxide gas.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: What is the primary objective of implementing clinical isolation for an infected patient?
back: To protect the community by separating infected persons or animals during the period of communicability to prevent direct or indirect transmission to susceptible hosts.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [The purpose of isolation is to protect the community by preventing transfer of infection from the reservoir to the possible susceptible hosts.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: How does early treatment act as a control mechanism to stop the spread of infectious agents?
back: It kills the pathogen within the reservoir before dissemination occurs, reducing communicability and shortening the overall duration of the infective period.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [The object of treatment is to kill the infectious agent when it is still in the reservoir, i.e., before it is disseminated. Treatment reduces the communicability of disease, cuts short the duration of illness and prevents development of secondary cases.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: Contrast isolation and quarantine regarding the health status of the individuals involved.
back: Isolation separates confirmed infected persons or carriers from others. Quarantine restricts the movement of healthy persons (well contacts) who were exposed to a disease.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page)/127: [Isolation is defined as “separation... of infected persons...” In contrast to isolation, quarantine applies to restrictions on the healthy contacts of an infectious disease.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: A pediatric patient presents with generalized itchy vesicles; when can their isolation safely be discontinued?
back: Isolation for Chickenpox is strictly required until all skin lesions have crusted, which typically occurs approximately six days after the rash onset.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [Chickenpox: Duration of Isolation: Until all lesions crusted; usually about 6 days after onset of rash.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: Which chemical agent is preferred for the sterilization of heat-sensitive respiratory equipment and endoscopes?
back: Glutaraldehyde is preferred as it is 10 times more effective than formaldehyde and less toxic; Ethylene oxide gas is also used for heat-sensitive surgical plastics.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Glutaraldehyde... In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes... Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: To which specific group of patients should healthcare workers apply Standard Precautions?
back: Standard precautions apply to all patients regardless of diagnosis to limit contact with all biological fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes, and non-intact skin.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Standard (routine) precautions should be applied to the care of all patients. This includes limiting health care worker contact with all secretions or biological fluids; skin lesions, mucous membranes, and blood or body fluids.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: Identify three proven effective measures for the prevention of Surgical Site Infections (SSIs).
back: 1. Optimal antibiotic prophylaxis. 2. Aseptic practice in the operating room. 3. Limiting preoperative hospital stay and using proper local skin preparation.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Surgical site infections: Proven effective: Surgical technique; Clean operating environment; Preoperative shower and local skin preparation; Optimal antibiotic prophylaxis; Aseptic practice in operating room.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: Differentiate between the usage criteria for Standard Isolation and High Security Isolation.
back: Standard isolation is determined by individual risk assessment. High security isolation is strictly reserved for infections where the risk of transmission is deemed exceptionally serious.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [There are several types of isolation — standard isolation... high security isolation... Today, isolation is recommended only when the risk of transmission of the infection is exceptionally serious.]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: Describe the three-component 'Chain of Transmission' loop targeted for disease control.
back: The loop consists of the reservoir (source), the route of transmission, and the susceptible host. Control aims to break the weakest link in this chain.
citation: Page 124 (Book Page)/125: [identify these weak points and break the weakest links in the chain of transmission... 1. The reservoir or source of infection 2. The route(s) of transmission 3. The susceptible host (people at risk).]

category: Discuss appropriate isolation and patient-care practices to prevent the spread of infectious agents
front: What are the standard physical parameters required for sterilization via autoclaving?
back: Exposure to saturated steam at a temperature of 121°C under 15 lb/in² of pressure for a duration of 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in for 15 minutes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Define sterilization in the context of medical microbiology.
back: The complete killing or removal of all forms of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, which are highly resistant.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: How does moist heat (autoclaving) differ from dry heat in protein denaturation?
back: Moist heat uses water to disrupt noncovalent hydrogen bonds, allowing sterilization at lower temperatures than dry heat.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [Moist heat sterilizes at a lower temperature than dry heat, because water aids in the disruption of noncovalent bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds), which hold protein chains together.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Distinguish disinfection from sterilization regarding bacterial spores.
back: Sterilization kills all life including spores; disinfection kills many pathogens but allows spores and some organisms to survive.
citation: Page 235 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing of all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is reducing the number of bacteria... Spores and some bacteria will survive.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Which chemical agent is required for sterilizing heat-sensitive surgical instruments like endoscopes?
back: Ethylene oxide gas (for plastics/instruments) or Glutaraldehyde (for endoscopes/respiratory equipment). Both alkylate proteins/nucleic acids.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials... Glutaraldehyde... is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Why is 70% ethanol preferred over 100% ethanol for skin antisepsis?
back: Maximal activity requires water to denature proteins and disorganize lipid membrane structures effectively.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: What are the standard physical parameters for effective autoclaving?
back: Exposure to steam at 121°C under 15 lb/in² (psi) pressure for 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Which antiseptic should be used specifically before obtaining blood cultures?
back: Iodine-containing compounds (tincture of iodine or iodophors), as alcohol is less effective against skin flora like S. epidermidis.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [because it is not as effective as iodine-containing compounds, the latter should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture and installing intravenous catheters.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: In intravenous solution preparation, why is filtration used if autoclaving also sterilizes?
back: Filtration removes heat-resistant endotoxins (pyrogens) from dead bacteria that cause fever in patients.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls of the dead gram-negative bacteria caused fever... Therefore, solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free prior to autoclaving.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Contrast the primary targets of UV light and X-rays in microorganisms.
back: UV light causes thymine dimers in DNA; X-rays produce free radicals that break covalent DNA bonds.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [lesion caused by UV irradiation is the formation of thymine dimers... X-rays have higher energy... and kill mainly by the production of free radicals.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Define medical antiseptics and provide two common examples.
back: Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes. Examples: 70% ethanol, iodine.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: What is the primary objective of adhering to transmission-based precautions?
back: To break the chain of transmission by identifying and eliminating the 'weakest link' between the infectious reservoir and the susceptible host.
citation: Page 124 (Book Page): [The basic approach in controlling disease is to identify these weak points and break the weakest links in the chain of transmission.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: How does thorough hand hygiene physiologically reduce the spread of healthcare-associated infections (HAIs)?
back: It interrupts the 'most common route' by removing transient pathogenic flora acquired through direct contact with patients or contaminated environment.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Contrast Standard Precautions with Transmission-Based Precautions in a clinical setting.
back: Standard: Applied universally to all patients for body fluid contact. Transmission-Based: Added specifically for patients with exceptionally serious risks (e.g., isolation).
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions should be applied to the care of all patients... Isolation is recommended only when the risk of transmission of the infection is exceptionally serious.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: A patient on a ventilator for 72 hours develops new radiological infiltrates and fever. What is the priority intervention?
back: Suspect Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP). Priorities: Aseptic intubation/suctioning, limiting ventilator duration, and strict adherence to infection control protocols.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Pneumonia: Ventilator-associated... Aseptic intubation and suctioning... Limit duration.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: What pharmacological step is effective in reducing nosocomial UTIs related to indwelling catheters?
back: Daily antiseptic perineal cleaning and the use of antimicrobial-coated catheters to prevent bacterial migration into the urinary tract.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Urinary tract infections. Limit duration... Daily antiseptic perineal cleaning... Antimicrobial-coated catheter.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: What are the specific temporal criteria for defining a Nosocomial or Hospital-Acquired Infection (HAI)?
back: Infections occurring more than 48 hours after admission that were neither present nor incubating at the time of patient entry.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Infections occurring more than 48 hours after admission are usually considered nosocomial.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Apply the concept of 'Barrier Nursing' to the reduction of cross-infection.
back: Uses physical barriers (PPE) and spatial separation to prevent transfer from the reservoir (infected case/carrier) to susceptible hosts.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Nursing techniques: Barrier nursing and task nursing have also been recommended to minimize cross infection.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Differentiate the clinical necessity of autoclaving over boiling for surgical instruments.
back: Autoclaving (121C at 15lb/in) achieves sterilization by killing heat-resistant spores, whereas boiling only disinfects and fails to eliminate spore-related HAIs.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [Because bacterial spores are resistant to boiling (100°C...)... steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in, reaches a temperature of 121°C... This kills even the highly heat-resistant spores.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: Describe the surveillance-action loop used by Infection Control Committees to reduce HAIs.
back: Monitors baseline infection rates, identifies unusual increases (outbreaks), investigates transmission source, and implements targeted isolation or disinfection policies.
citation: Page 365 (Book Page): [Strengthening epidemiological surveillance and drug-resistance surveillance mechanisms... for early detection, confirmation and communication.]

category: Explain the importance of adherence to transmission-based precautions in reducing healthcare-associated infections
front: What chemical property makes 70% ethanol a high-yield antiseptic for hand hygiene?
back: It disorganizes lipid structures in cell membranes and denatures proteins, requiring a water component for maximal antimicrobial efficacy.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol... acts mainly by disorganizing the lipid structure in membranes, but it denatures proteins as well. Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Differentiate between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization based on microbial outcome.
back:
* Cleaning: Physical removal of visible soil/organic matter (e.g., using water/detergents).
* Disinfection: Destruction of most pathogens; however, highly resistant bacterial spores usually survive.
* Sterilization: Absolute destruction or removal of all microbial life, including spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Contrast the standard mechanism and sporicidal efficacy of autoclaving versus chemical disinfection.
back:
* Autoclaving (Sterilization): Uses moist heat (121°C/15psi for 15 mins) to denature proteins; 100% sporicidal.
* Chemical Disinfection: Disrupts cell membranes or modifies proteins (e.g., alcohols/phenols); lacks reliable efficacy against bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in for 15 minutes. Disinfectants vary... act primarily by one of the three mechanisms: (1) disruption of the lipid-containing cell membrane, (2) modification of proteins, or (3) modification of DNA.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the primary microbiological definition of sterilization?
back:
- Killing or removal of all microorganisms.
- Includes destruction of highly resistant bacterial spores.
- Essential for surgical instruments and intravenous solutions.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, which are highly resistant.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: By what biochemical mechanism does moist heat achieve microbial destruction during autoclaving?
back:
- Denaturation of proteins.
- Disruption of noncovalent bonds (hydrogen bonds).
- Destabilizes secondary and tertiary protein structures.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): In general, heat kills by denaturing proteins, but membrane damage and enzymatic cleavage of DNA may also be involved. Moist heat... aids in the disruption of noncovalent bonds.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Contrast the clinical application of disinfectants versus antiseptics.
back:
- Disinfectants: Applied to inanimate objects (e.g., floors/equipment); may be corrosive.
- Antiseptics: Non-toxic chemicals safe for skin and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): Disinfectants vary in their tissue-damaging properties... to less toxic materials such as ethanol and iodine, which can be used on skin surfaces. Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which sterilization method is indicated for surgical plastics and heat-sensitive instruments?
back:
- Ethylene oxide gas.
- Kills via alkylation of proteins and nucleic acids.
- Avoids damage caused by high-temperature moist heat.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics. It kills by alkylating both proteins and nucleic acids.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: How do heavy metals like silver nitrate specifically inhibit bacterial growth?
back:
- Binding to sulfhydryl (-SH) groups.
- Blocking essential enzymatic activity.
- Common in silver sulfadiazine for burn infections.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): They act by binding to sulfhydryl groups, thereby blocking enzymatic activity. Silver sulfadiazine is used to prevent infection of burn wounds.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the formal microbiological definition of 'Death' in microorganisms?
back:
- Irreversible inability to reproduce.
- Quantified by lack of colony formation in culture.
- Distinct from physical presence of dead remains (endotoxins).
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): Death is defined as the inability to reproduce... The relationship is usually stated in terms of survivors because they are easily measured by colony formation.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol clinically superior to 100% ethanol for skin disinfection?
back:
- Requires water for maximal protein denaturation.
- Water facilitates penetration of the cell membrane.
- 100% ethanol causes rapid surface dehydration preventing deep killing.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Compare the sterilization requirements for heat-stable instruments versus heat-sensitive intravenous solutions.
back:
- Instruments: Autoclaving (121°C/15min) to kill spores.
- IV Solutions: Filtration (0.22 μm) to ensure they are pyrogen-free.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): Filtration is the preferred method of sterilizing certain solutions... heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls of the dead gram-negative bacteria caused fever... solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What mathematical relationship defines the rate of microbial killing by chemical agents?
back:
- Inversely proportionate to survivors (N).
- Directly proportionate to Concentration (C) × Time (T).
- Collectively referred to as the 'dose'.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): The number of survivors, N, is inversely proportionate to the concentration of the agent, C, and to the time of application of the agent, T. Collectively, CT is often referred to as the dose.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: State the standard temperature and pressure requirements for effective autoclaving.
back:
- Temperature: 121°C.
- Pressure: 15 lb/in².
- Time: 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): For this purpose, an autoclave chamber is used in which steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in², reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Distinguish briefly between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization.
back:
* Cleaning: Physical removal of organic matter/debris.
* Disinfection: Killing many/most pathogens; spores often survive.
* Sterilization: Complete destruction/removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the mechanism and standard parameters for moist heat sterilization (autoclaving)?
back:
* Mechanism: Denaturation of proteins and disruption of noncovalent bonds.
* Parameters: 121°C at 15 lb/in² pressure for 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in² for 15 minutes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: How do disinfectants and antiseptics differ by site of application?
back:
* Disinfectants: Used on inanimate/non-living objects (e.g., floors, instruments).
* Antiseptics: Milder chemicals safe for skin and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which sterilization method is mandatory for heat-sensitive surgical plastics and sutures?
back:
* Ethylene oxide gas (alkylates proteins/nucleic acids).
* Alternatively, X-ray radiation (produces free radicals).
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [X-rays are used in medicine for sterilization of heat-sensitive items, such as sutures and surgical gloves, and plastic items, such as syringes.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol more effective than 100% ethanol for disinfection?
back:
* Water is required for maximal protein denaturation activity.
* Acts by disorganizing membrane lipids and denaturing proteins.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the specific filter pore size required to achieve sterility in IV solutions?
back:
* 0.22 μm.
* This size retains all bacteria and bacterial spores.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [The most commonly used filter is composed of nitrocellulose and has a pore size of 0.22 μm. This size will retain all bacteria and spores.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What determines the 'Rate of Killing' of microorganisms by chemical agents?
back:
* Product of Concentration (C) and Time (T).
* Survivors (N) are inversely proportionate to CT (Dose).
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [The rate of killing is defined by the relationship N α 1/CT... the number of survivors, N, is inversely proportionate to the concentration of the agent, C, and to the time of application of the agent, T.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is iodine preferred over alcohol for skin preparation before blood cultures?
back:
* Alcohol is not as effective as iodine compounds against skin flora (e.g., S. epidermidis).
* Prevents false-positive culture contamination.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [However, because it is not as effective as iodine-containing compounds, the latter should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture and installing intravenous catheters.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the mechanism of UV light-induced microbial death?
back:
* Wavelength: 250–260 nm.
* Mechanism: Formation of thymine dimers in DNA, inhibiting replication.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [The most significant lesion caused by UV irradiation is the formation of thymine dimers... DNA replication is inhibited and the organism cannot grow.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which organism is used as a biological indicator for autoclave effectiveness?
back: * Spore-forming organisms (e.g., members of genus Clostridium).
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [To test the effectiveness of the autoclaving process, spore-forming organisms, such as members of the genus Clostridium, are used.]

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the primary defining difference between sterilization and disinfection?
back:
- Sterilization: Killing or removal of ALL microorganisms, including highly resistant bacterial spores.
- Disinfection: Killing of MANY but not all; pathogens die, but some organisms/spores survive.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, which are highly resistant... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: How does moist heat (autoclaving) facilitate protein denaturation more effectively than dry heat?
back:
- Water aids in disrupting noncovalent (hydrogen) bonds.
- This allows proteins to denature at lower temperatures compared to dry heat.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): Moist heat sterilizes at a lower temperature than dry heat, because water aids in the disruption of noncovalent bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds), which hold protein chains together.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Contrast the outcome of bacterial spores when subjected to boiling versus autoclaving.
back:
- Boiling (100°C): Spores are resistant and survive.
- Autoclaving (121°C): Increased pressure allows higher temperatures that kill spores.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): Because bacterial spores are resistant to boiling (100°C at sea level), they must be exposed to a higher temperature; this cannot be achieved unless the pressure is increased.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Which sterilization method is appropriate for heat-sensitive surgical instruments like endoscopes?
back:
- Ethylene oxide gas (sterilization via alkylation).
- Glutaraldehyde (10x more effective and less toxic than formaldehyde).
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments... Glutaraldehyde... is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol more effective than 100% ethanol for skin antisepsis?
back:
- Maximal activity requires water to aid in protein denaturation.
- It acts by disorganizing lipid structures in membranes.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%). It acts mainly by disorganizing the lipid structure in membranes, but it denatures proteins as well.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: State the standard parameters required for effective moist heat sterilization in an autoclave.
back:
- Temperature: 121°C.
- Pressure: 15 lb/in².
- Time: 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in² for 15 minutes.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Why is filtration chosen over autoclaving for intravenous solutions?
back:
- Prevents pyrogen-induced fever caused by heat-resistant endotoxins.
- 0.22 μm nitrocellulose filters physically retain all bacteria and spores.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls of the dead gram-negative bacteria caused fever in recipients... Therefore, solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free prior to autoclaving.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Before drawing blood cultures, why is Iodine preferred over Alcohol for skin preparation?
back:
- Iodine is more effective against skin flora like S. epidermidis.
- Ensures contamination does not yield false-positive culture results.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): Iodine is the most effective skin antiseptic... should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture... because contamination with skin flora such as Staphylococcus epidermidis can be a problem.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: What is the primary molecular lesion caused by Ultraviolet (UV) light irradiation in bacteria?
back:
- Formation of thymine dimers in DNA.
- Inhibits DNA replication and prevents microbial growth.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): The most significant lesion caused by UV irradiation is the formation of thymine dimers... As a result, DNA replication is inhibited and the organism cannot grow.

category: Distinguish between cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization
front: Q: Define 'antiseptics' and distinguish them from general disinfectants.
back:
- Antiseptics: Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on living tissues (skin/mucous membranes).
- Disinfectants: Generally more toxic/corrosive; used primarily on inanimate objects.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics... disinfectants vary... from the corrosive phenol-containing compounds... to less toxic materials such as ethanol.

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: What is the fundamental difference between sterilization and disinfection?
back:
* Sterilization: Kills all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores.
* Disinfection: Kills many pathogens but allows survival of some organisms and resistant spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of action for alcohols (ethanol) in disinfection?
back:
* Disorganizes lipid structures in cell membranes.
* Denatures cellular proteins.
* Requires water for maximal efficacy (optimal at 70%).
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Alcohol... acts mainly by disorganizing the lipid structure in membranes, but it denatures proteins as well. Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Contrast the clinical usage of disinfectants versus antiseptics.
back:
* Disinfectants: Corrosive/toxic; strictly for inanimate objects (e.g., phenol).
* Antiseptics: Non-toxic; safe for skin and mucous membranes (e.g., ethanol/iodine).
citation: Page 228 (Book Page)-229: [Disinfectants... should be used only on inanimate objects... Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Which sterilization method is indicated for heat-sensitive surgical plastics and endoscopes?
back:
* Ethylene oxide gas: For surgical instruments/plastics damaged by heat.
* Glutaraldehyde: High-level disinfectant used for endoscopes and respiratory equipment.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page)/232: [Surgical instruments that can be damaged by moist heat are usually sterilized by exposure to ethylene oxide gas... Glutaraldehyde... is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol more clinically effective as an antiseptic than 100% ethanol?
back:
* Absolute alcohol lacks the water necessary for protein denaturation.
* Hydration facilitates the penetration and destruction of the cell membrane/proteins.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: What are the standard physical parameters for effective autoclaving?
back:
* Temperature: 121°C.
* Pressure: 15 lb/in².
* Duration: 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [For this purpose, an autoclave chamber is used in which steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in2, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: When is filtration preferred over autoclaving for clinical solutions?
back:
* Heat-sensitive intravenous solutions.
* Prevention of pyrogen-induced fevers caused by dead Gram-negative endotoxins.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [Filtration is the preferred method of sterilizing certain solutions... heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls of the dead gram-negative bacteria caused fever... solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Which chemicals are the most effective for skin preparation prior to blood cultures?
back:
* Iodine-containing compounds (Iodophors/Tincture of Iodine).
* Rationale: Superior to alcohol in killing S. epidermidis/skin flora contamination.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Iodine is the most effective skin antiseptic used in medical practice and should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture... Iodophors are complexes of iodine with detergents.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: How do Chlorine and Iodine act as disinfectants at the molecular level?
back:
* Powerful oxidizing agents.
* Cross-link/inactivate essential sulfhydryl groups in enzymes.
* Form inactive disulfide bonds.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Chlorine is a powerful oxidizing agent that kills by cross-linking essential sulfhydryl groups in enzymes... Iodine... inactivates sulfhydryl-containing enzymes.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: What are the target pathogens of milk pasteurization (62°C for 30 minutes)?
back:
* Mycobacterium bovis.
* Salmonella.
* Brucella and Listeria.
* Note: Kills vegetative cells but does not achieve sterilization.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [Pasteurization... is sufficient to kill the vegetative cells of the milk-borne pathogens (e.g., Mycobacterium bovis, Salmonella, Streptococcus, Listeria, and Brucella), but not to sterilize the milk.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Define disinfection and how it differs from sterilization.
back:
• Disinfection: Kills many, but not all microorganisms; bacterial spores may survive.
• Sterilization: Kills all microorganisms, including highly resistant bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: What determines the 'Rate of Killing' (N) for microorganisms?
back:
• Inversely proportionate to concentration (C) and time (T).
• Formula: N ∝ 1/CT.
• Dose is collectively referred to as CT.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [Death of microorganisms occurs at a certain rate dependent primarily on two variables: the concentration of the killing agent and the length of time... N α 1/CT... collectively, CT is often referred to as the dose.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Distinguish between disinfectants and antiseptics in clinical practice.
back:
• Disinfectants: Used for inanimate objects (too toxic/caustic for tissue).
• Antiseptics: Used on skin and mucous membranes (lower toxicity).
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics. Disinfectants... should be used only on inanimate objects.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Choose the correct sterilization method for heat-sensitive surgical plastics and endoscopes.
back:
• Plastics/Instruments: Ethylene oxide gas.
• Endoscopes/Respiratory equipment: Glutaraldehyde (10x more effective than formaldehyde).
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Glutaraldehyde... In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes... Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Why is 70% ethanol more effective as an antiseptic than 100% ethanol?
back:
• Requires water for maximal protein denaturation.
• Acts by disorganizing lipid structures in cell membranes.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%)... It acts mainly by disorganizing the lipid structure in membranes, but it denatures proteins as well.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Specify the exact parameters for standard autoclave sterilization.
back:
• Temperature: 121°C.
• Pressure: 15 lb/in².
• Time: 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [Moist heat sterilization, usually autoclaving... steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in2, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: In which clinical scenario is iodine preferred over ethanol for skin prep?
back:
• Prior to blood culture collection or IV catheter installation.
• Reason: More effective against skin flora like Staphylococcus epidermidis.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Seventy percent ethanol is often used... prior to venipuncture. However, because it is not as effective as iodine-containing compounds, the latter should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture and installing intravenous catheters.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Which pathogen is notably resistant to the 2% NaOH used for sputum liquefaction?
back:
• Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• Note: Mycobacteria are relatively resistant to acids and alkalis used in clinical labs.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Strong acids and alkalis kill by denaturing proteins. Although most bacteria are susceptible, it is important to note that Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other mycobacteria are relatively resistant to 2% NaOH.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Explain the role of chlorine and hypochlorite in public health disinfection.
back:
• Mechanism: Powerful oxidant; cross-links sulfhydryl groups to inactivate enzymes.
• Use: Purification of water supply and hospital/home disinfectant (bleach).
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Chlorine is used as a disinfectant to purify the water supply... active component of hypochlorite (bleach)... powerful oxidizing agent that kills by cross-linking essential sulfhydryl groups in enzymes.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: What is the standard pore size for bacterial filtration, and why is it used?
back:
• Pore size: 0.22 μm.
• Use: Sterilizing heat-sensitive liquids and producing pyrogen-free IV solutions.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [The most commonly used filter... has a pore size of 0.22 μm. This size will retain all bacteria and spores... solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free prior to autoclaving.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Define the primary difference between sterilization and disinfection regarding microbial life.
back:
• Sterilization: Kills all forms including bacterial spores.
• Disinfection: Kills many pathogens but spares some organisms and spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol more effective than 100% ethanol for skin disinfection?
back:
• Ethanol requires water for maximal activity to denature proteins.
• Effectively disorganizes lipid structures in cell membranes.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Distinguish between Disinfectants and Antiseptics based on application site.
back:
• Disinfectants: Toxic/corrosive; used only on inanimate objects (e.g., floors).
• Antiseptics: Low toxicity; safe for skin and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page)-229: [phenol-containing compounds, which should be used only on inanimate objects, to less toxic materials... used on skin surfaces. Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Scenario: A gastroscope enters a mucous membrane but not sterile tissue. What level of processing is required?
back:
• High-Level Disinfection (HLD).
• Specifically requires glutaraldehyde to kill vegetative cells and some spores.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Glutaraldehyde... In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes, and hemodialysis equipment.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: What is the biochemical mechanism by which Chlorine (Bleach) kills pathogens?
back:
• Acts as a powerful oxidizing agent.
• Cross-links essential sulfhydryl groups in enzymes to form inactive disulfides.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Chlorine is a powerful oxidizing agent that kills by cross-linking essential sulfhydryl groups in enzymes to form the inactive disulfide.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: List the standard physical parameters for sterilization by autoclaving.
back:
• Temperature: 121°C.
• Pressure: 15 lb/in².
• Time: 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in for 15 minutes. This kills even the highly heat-resistant spores.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Why must iodine be used instead of alcohol before obtaining a blood culture?
back:
• Iodine is the most effective skin antiseptic.
• Prevents contamination by deep skin flora like Staphylococcus epidermidis.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Iodine is the most effective skin antiseptic used in medical practice and should be used prior to obtaining a blood culture... because contamination with skin flora such as Staphylococcus epidermidis can be a problem.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Differential: Contrast the processing of a surgical scalpel versus a stethoscope.
back:
• Scalpel: Critical item; requires full sterilization (autoclave).
• Stethoscope: Non-critical item; requires low-level disinfection (e.g., 70% alcohol).
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving... Surgical instruments... are usually sterilized...]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: How do quaternary ammonium compounds (e.g., Benzalkonium chloride) disrupt bacteria?
back:
• Act as surfactants (detergents).
• Interact with membrane lipids via hydrophobic chains to disrupt the lipid bilayer.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [These surfactants interact with the lipid in the cell membrane through their hydrophobic chain and with the surrounding water through their polar group and thus disrupt the membrane.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Which chemical agent is the preferred 'sterilant' for heat-sensitive surgical plastics?
back:
• Ethylene oxide gas.
• Kills by alkylating essential amino and hydroxyl groups in proteins/nucleic acids.

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Distinguish between sterilization and disinfection based on their efficacy against bacterial spores.
back: Sterilization: Complete destruction of all microorganisms, including highly resistant bacterial spores. Disinfection: Eliminates many pathogens but may leave spores or certain organisms intact. Sterilization is mandatory for invasive surgical instruments, while disinfection is appropriate for non-critical inanimate surfaces.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice
front: Q: Why is glutaraldehyde clinically prioritized for disinfecting heat-sensitive instruments like endoscopes?
back: Glutaraldehyde is ten times more effective and significantly less toxic than formaldehyde. It achieves high-level disinfection by alkylating essential microbial proteins and nucleic acids, making it the preferred choice for delicate, heat-sensitive equipment including endoscopes and respiratory therapy devices.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Glutaraldehyde, which has two reactive aldehyde groups, is 10 times more effective than formaldehyde and is less toxic. In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes, and hemodialysis equipment.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice

• Alcohol/Iodine: Less toxic; suitable as antiseptics for skin and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [phenol-containing compounds, which should be used only on inanimate objects, to less toxic materials such as ethanol and iodine, which can be used on skin surfaces.]

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice

category: Describe the levels of disinfection and their relevance in clinical practice

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications

• Filtration physically removes cell wall fragments
• Filtration ensures solutions are pyrogen-free
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): In the past, solutions for intravenous use were autoclaved, but heat-resistant endotoxin in the cell walls of the dead gram-negative bacteria caused fever... solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol preferred over 100% ethanol as a skin antiseptic?
back:
• Requires water for maximal activity
• Efficiently denatures proteins and disrupts membrane lipids
• Used prior to venipuncture/immunization
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Q: What standard pore size is required in nitrocellulose filters to retain all bacteria and spores?
back:
• 0.22 μm
• Retains particles via physical trapping and electrostatic attraction
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): The most commonly used filter is composed of nitrocellulose and has a pore size of 0.22 μm. This size will retain all bacteria and spores.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Q: What are the standard temperature and pressure requirements for effective sterilization by autoclaving?
back: - Temperature: 121°C. - Pressure: 15 lb/in². - Duration: 15–20 minutes. - Outcome: Eradicates all microbial life, including bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): "Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in² for 15 minutes."

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Q: Which sterilization agent is preferred for heat-sensitive endoscopes and what is its primary biochemical mechanism?
back: - Agent: Glutaraldehyde. - Mechanism: Alkylation of protein and nucleic acid chemical groups. - Indication: Endoscopes, respiratory equipment, and hemodialysis tools.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): "Glutaraldehyde... In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes, and hemodialysis equipment."

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: What are the standard physical parameters required for effective sterilization via autoclaving?
back:
• Temperature: 121°C
• Pressure: 15 lb/in²
• Duration: 15 to 20 minutes
• Kills all microbes including spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization] consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in2 for 15 minutes.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: How does moist heat achieve microbial death more effectively than dry heat?
back:
• Aids disruption of noncovalent bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds).
• Denatures proteins at lower temperatures.
• Facilitates structural collapse of protein secondary and tertiary structures.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): Moist heat sterilizes at a lower temperature than dry heat, because water aids in the disruption of noncovalent bonds... which hold protein chains together.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Contrast sterilization and disinfection regarding the elimination of bacterial spores.
back:
• Sterilization: Complete removal/killing of all life forms, including highly resistant spores.
• Disinfection: Kills many pathogens but spores and some organisms typically survive.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all... bacterial spores may survive.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Which sterilization method is indicated for high-precision plastic instruments and heat-sensitive surgical items?
back:
• Ethylene oxide gas.
• Alkylates proteins and nucleic acids.
• Suitable for materials damaged by moist heat (e.g., plastics, certain metals).
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): Surgical instruments that can be damaged by moist heat are usually sterilized by exposure to ethylene oxide gas.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: What is the biochemical step by which Chlorine and Iodine act as disinfectants?
back:
• Act as powerful oxidizing agents.
• Cross-link essential sulfhydryl (-SH) groups in enzymes.
• Form inactive disulfide bonds, inhibiting enzymatic function.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): Chlorine is a powerful oxidizing agent... cross-linking essential sulfhydryl groups... Iodine, like chlorine, is an oxidant that inactivates sulfhydryl-containing enzymes.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Which organism is utilized as the standard biological indicator to verify autoclave sterilization efficacy?
back:
• Spore-forming members of the genus Clostridium.
• Selected due to high heat resistance of their spores.
• Successful kill confirms sterilization parameters were met.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): To test the effectiveness of the autoclaving process, spore-forming organisms, such as members of the genus Clostridium, are used.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Why is 70% ethanol more effective than 100% ethanol for skin antisepsis?
back:
• Denaturation of proteins requires water for maximal activity.
• 100% alcohol causes rapid surface coagulation, preventing penetration.
• 70% allows deeper penetration and disorganization of cell membranes.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Identify the indicated method for sterilizing intravenous fluids containing heat-labile components.
back:
• Filtration via nitrocellulose filters.
• Pore size: 0.22 μm.
• Physically retains all bacteria and spores; removes heat-resistant endotoxins.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): Filtration is the preferred method of sterilizing certain solutions (e.g., those with heat-sensitive components).

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Describe the metabolic inhibition loop caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation in microbes.
back:
• Absorption by purine/pyrimidine bases (250-260 nm).
• Induces formation of thymine dimers.
• Halts DNA replication, preventing growth and reproduction.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): The most significant lesion caused by UV irradiation is the formation of thymine dimers... DNA replication is inhibited and the organism cannot grow.

category: Identify commonly used sterilization methods and their indications
front: Which chemical agent is indicated for the sterilization of endoscopes and respiratory equipment?
back:
• Glutaraldehyde.
• Possesses two reactive aldehyde groups.
• 10 times more effective than formaldehyde and significantly less toxic.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): Glutaraldehyde... In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes, and hemodialysis equipment.

category: Explain the importance of proper instrument handling to prevent hospital-acquired infections and surgical site infections
front: Q: Define sterilization in the context of hospital instrument processing.
back: The complete killing or removal of all forms of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, which are highly resistant.]

category: Explain the importance of proper instrument handling to prevent hospital-acquired infections and surgical site infections
front: Q: Why is moist heat (autoclaving) more efficient than dry heat for instrument sterilization?
