category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Identify a 'coal-face' error related to antibiotic use that compromises surgical patient safety.
back: Prophylaxis errors. These include inappropriate timing, wrong drug choice, or excessive duration of administration.
citation: Page 264 (Book Page): [Cuschieri and others have described coal-face errors... include: prophylaxis errors; prescription/parenteral administration errors.]

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: What is the primary ecological consequence of intense antibiotic use in hospital environments regarding HAIs?
back: The selective pressure of intense antibiotic use promotes antibiotic resistance among microorganisms, complicating Healthcare-Associated Infection (HAI) management.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): The selective pressure of intense antibiotic use promotes antibiotic resistance.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: How does inadequate or inappropriate antibiotic treatment physically lead to antimicrobial resistance?
back: It induces drug resistance in the infectious agent, enabling survival of resistant strains and frustrating disease control attempts via chemotherapy.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): If the treatment is inadequate or inappropriate, it may induce drug resistance in the infectious agent and may frustrate attempts to control the disease by chemotherapy.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: Once a pathogen for Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia is identified, what is the recommended adjustment to therapy?
back: Antibiotic therapy should be refined to use the narrowest possible spectrum agent(s) to prevent broader ecological resistance.
citation: Page 561 (Book Page): If the infecting organism is identified, antibiotic therapy should be refined, with the narrowest possible spectrum agent(s) being used.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: In a patient with long-term catheterization, why is 'limiting duration' prioritized over systemic prophylaxis to prevent AMR?
back: Limiting duration reduces colonization risk; systemic prophylaxis for catheters is 'proven not effective' and actively promotes antimicrobial resistance.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): Urinary tract infections: Proven effective: Limit duration of catheter... Proven not effective: Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: What specific local data must guide the choice of initial empirical antibiotic therapy in HAIs?
back: Knowledge of local patterns of microbiology and specific regional antibiotic resistance patterns.
citation: Page 561 (Book Page): The initial choice of empirical antibiotic therapy is considerably more challenging, however, given the diversity of pathogens and the potential for drug resistance... appropriately guided by knowledge of local patterns of microbiology and antibiotic resistance.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: Why is early diagnosis of infection considered the 'cornerstone' of rational antibiotic use?
back: It allows prompt, specific treatment of the 'spark' (index cases) before the need for prolonged or multi-drug broad-spectrum regimens arises.
citation: Page 125 (Book Page): Early diagnosis... is the cornerstone on which the edifice of disease control is built... prompt detection of cases (and carriers) and their treatment is like stamping out the “spark” rather than calling the fire brigade.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: Apply the principle of 'Selective Decontamination of the Digestive Tract' (SDD) to antibiotic resistance prevention.
back: It involves decontaminating the upper airway/gut with oral antiseptics (e.g., 2% Chlorhexidine) to prevent colonization by multi-drug resistant pathogens in ICU patients.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): Oral antiseptic (chlorhexidine 2%) may be used to decontaminate the upper airway and some intensive care units employ selective decontamination of the digestive tract.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: A ventilated patient shows new lung infiltrates. Why is microbiological confirmation prioritized over immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics?
back: To differentiate infection from non-infectious conditions (e.g., ARDS, embolism). Prevents unnecessary antibiotic exposure and resulting resistance pressure.
citation: Page 561 (Book Page): Microbiological confirmation should be sought whenever possible... raising a broad differential diagnosis that includes pulmonary embolism, ARDS, pulmonary oedema.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: How does the irrational use of Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) indirectly lead to antibiotic resistance in hospitals?
back: PPIs reduce gastric acidity, facilitating bacterial colonization and increasing HAP risk, which necessitates further antibiotic use and induces resistance.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): Steps should be taken to minimise the chances of aspiration and to limit the use of stress ulcer prophylaxis with proton pump inhibitors.

category: Relate the importance of rational antibiotic use in preventing antimicrobial resistance linked to HAIs
front: Q: Identify a common prescribing error that contributes to sub-therapeutic dosing and antimicrobial resistance in surgical wards.
back: Dosage calculation errors and inadequate knowledge of specific medications or their interactions.
citation: Page 264 (Book Page): Common medication errors include: poor assessment or inadequate knowledge of patients... inadequate knowledge of the medications; dosage calculation errors.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the most critical behavioral measure for the surgical team to prevent transmission of HAIs?
back: Hand hygiene. It is the most common route of infection. Use soap and water or alcohol-based disinfectants as part of the 'Clean Care is Safer Care' initiative.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Why is preoperative shaving no longer recommended for surgical site infection (SSI) prophylaxis?
back: It is proven 'not effective' and may increase infection risk through skin abrasions. If hair removal is necessary, clipping or preoperative showers are preferred.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Table 2: Proven not effective: Preoperative shaving.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Distinguish between disinfectants and antiseptics in the surgical clinical environment.
back: Disinfectants are for inanimate objects (caustic). Antiseptics (e.g., Chlorhexidine, Ethanol) are safe for skin and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 229 (Book Page): [Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on the surface of skin and mucous membranes are called antiseptics.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which three critical communication steps occur during the 'Before Skin Incision' phase of the Surgical Safety Checklist?
back: 1. Team introductions (name/role). 2. Confirm patient identity/site. 3. Review anticipated critical events (blood loss, sterility, anesthesia concerns).
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [Confirm all team members have introduced themselves by name and role. Confirm the patient’s name, procedure, and where the incision will be made. Anticipated Critical Events... To Surgeon: What is the anticipated blood loss?]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the optimal UHS-standard timing for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis administration?
back: Within 60 minutes prior to the surgical incision. This ensures adequate tissue concentrations of the antibiotic during the procedure.
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [Has antibiotic prophylaxis been given within the last 60 minutes?]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What clinical signs define a Surgical Site Infection (SSI) according to simplified surveillance criteria?
back: Any purulent discharge, abscess formation, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site occurring within one month of the operation.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How should a surgical team sterilize heat-sensitive instruments like plastics and specialized optics?
back: Ethylene oxide gas. It kills by alkylating proteins and nucleic acids, making it suitable for heat-sensitive surgical materials.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Contrast the clinical use of Chlorhexidine versus Iodophors in surgery.
back: Chlorhexidine is primarily used for the 'surgical scrub' (hand disinfection). Iodophors are complexes used for preparing the patient's skin site (less irritating).
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Chlorhexidine is a chlorinated phenol that is widely used as a hand disinfectant prior to surgery (“surgical scrub”)... Iodophors... are frequently used to prepare the skin prior to surgery.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What are the specific parameters required for autoclaving to ensure the destruction of resistant bacterial spores?
back: Exposure to moist heat (steam) at 121°C under 15 lb/in² pressure for 15–20 minutes. This provides a margin of safety for highly resistant spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in for 15 minutes.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which PPE components are mandatory for the surgical team under standard (routine) precautions?
back: Gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection. These are used to limit contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, and mucous membranes.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Health care workers must wear gloves for each contact which may lead to contamination, and also gown, mask and eye protection if contamination of clothes or the face is anticipated.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the most common route of microorganism transmission the surgical team must mitigate?
back:
• Direct contact via the hands of staff.
• Prevention: Strict adherence to WHO 'Clean Care is Safer Care' hand hygiene and alcohol-based disinfectants.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Why should the surgical team avoid preoperative shaving to prevent Surgical Site Infections (SSIs)?
back:
• Shaving is 'proven not effective' and increases infection risk via skin micro-trauma.
• Recommended: Preoperative showering and limiting preoperative hospital stay.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): Surgical site infections... Proven not effective: Preoperative shaving. Proven effective: Preoperative shower and local skin preparation.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Define the clinical timeframe required to classify a post-operative respiratory infection as HAP.
back:
• Onset must be at least 48 hours after hospital admission.
• The infection must not have been incubating at the time of admission.
citation: Page 560 (Book Page): Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined as an episode of pneumonia that presents at least 48 hours after admission to hospital and was not incubating at the time of admission.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How does limiting proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) help the surgical team prevent VAP?
back:
• PPIs increase gastric pH, promoting bacterial colonization.
• This increases the risk of aspirating infected gastric secretions into the lower respiratory tract.
citation: Page 561 (Book Page): Steps should be taken to minimise the chances of aspiration and to limit the use of stress ulcer prophylaxis with proton pump inhibitors.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which pharmacological agent is specifically recommended for oropharyngeal decontamination in ventilated surgical patients?
back:
• Oral antiseptic using 2% Chlorhexidine.
• Used to reduce upper airway microbial load and prevent micro-aspiration.
citation: Page 561 (Book Page): Oral antiseptic (chlorhexidine 2%) may be used to decontaminate the upper airway.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What are the three simplified clinical signs of a Surgical Site Infection (SSI)?
back:
• Any purulent discharge.
• Abscess formation.
• Spreading cellulitis at the site within one month of surgery.
citation: Page 365 (Book Page): Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Identify the three mandatory time points for utilizing the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.
back:
• 1. Before induction of anesthesia (Sign In).
• 2. Before skin incision (Time Out).
• 3. Before the patient leaves the operating room (Sign Out).
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): The surgical safety checklist identifies specific checks to be carried out at three obligatory time points (Figure 15.1).

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: A post-op patient develops fever and purulent sputum after 72 hours. Which criteria confirm VAP?
back:
• New radiological infiltrate on chest X-ray.
• Purulent sputum or increased oxygen requirements.
• Core temperature >38.3°C and leukocytosis.
citation: Page 560 (Book Page): The diagnosis should be considered in any hospitalised patient who develops purulent sputum... new radiological infiltrates... core temperature >38.3°C, and a leucocytosis.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How does endotracheal intubation bypass natural host defenses to increase infection risk?
back:
• It bypasses mucociliary clearance and the glottis.
• Provides a direct route for bacteria to enter the lower respiratory tract via aspiration.
citation: Page 561 (Book Page): Bacteria introduced into lower respiratory tract: Endotracheal intubation/tracheostomy... Aspiration of nasopharyngeal or gastric secretions.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the required sterilization method for heat-sensitive surgical instruments like endoscopes?
back:
• Exposure to Ethylene Oxide gas.
• This prevents damage caused by the high temperatures of autoclaving (121°C).
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): Surgical instruments that can be damaged by moist heat are usually sterilized by exposure to ethylene oxide gas.

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which administrative body within a hospital is responsible for formulating specific policies to control HAIs?
back:
- Hospital "Control of Infection Committee".
- Formulates policies on admissions, isolation, disinfection, and staff compliance monitoring.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Administrative measures : There should be a hospital “Control of Infection Committee” to formulate policies regarding admission of infectious cases, isolation facilities, disinfection procedures, and in fact all matters relating to control of hospital acquired infection.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What are the three physical parameters required for standard surgical sterilization via autoclaving?
back:
- Temperature: 121°C.
- Pressure: 15 lb/in².
- Time: 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in for 15 minutes.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Distinguish between sterilization and disinfection regarding the survival of bacterial spores.
back:
- Sterilization: Kills all forms of life, including resistant bacterial spores.
- Disinfection: Kills many pathogens, but bacterial spores often survive.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms... some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: A surgeon plans hair removal for an elective surgery. Which practice is proven ineffective for preventing SSIs?
back:
- Preoperative shaving is proven not effective.
- Recommended: Avoid hair removal or use clippers to prevent skin micro-abrasions.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Table 2: Surgical site infections... Proven not effective: Preoperative shaving.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which chlorinated phenol is the agent of choice for a preoperative 'surgical scrub' of hands?
back:
- Chlorhexidine.
- Preferred for hand disinfection due to being less caustic than pure phenol and having sustained activity.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Chlorhexidine is a chlorinated phenol that is widely used as a hand disinfectant prior to surgery (“surgical scrub”) and in the cleansing of wounds.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: List the three clinical criteria used to identify a Surgical Site Infection (SSI) post-operation.
back:
- Purulent discharge from the site.
- Abscess formation.
- Spreading cellulitis at the surgical site (within one month).
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Table 1: Simplified criteria for surveillance of nosocomial infections... Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Under Standard Precautions, how must the surgical team manage patient-care equipment between uses?
back:
- Discard single-use items.
- Disinfect or sterilize reusable items between every patient use.
- Promptly clean spills of infective material.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Ensure that patient-care equipment, supplies and linen contaminated with infective material is either discarded, or disinfected or sterilized between each patient use.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Regarding vascular device infections, which practice is proven ineffective for prophylaxis during catheter insertion?
back:
- Using antimicrobial creams for skin preparation.
- Proven effective measures include aseptic technique and limiting duration.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Table 2: Vascular device infections... Proven not effective: Antimicrobial creams for skin preparation.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How does the 'selective pressure' of a hospital environment contribute to the development of HAIs?
back:
- Intense antibiotic use promotes antibiotic resistance.
- Immunocompromised patients are exposed to high-load resistant microorganisms via staff hands or dust.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [The selective pressure of intense antibiotic use promotes antibiotic resistance... hospitalized patients are often immunocompromised... environment may facilitate the transmission of microorganisms among patients.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which gaseous agent is mandatory for the sterilization of heat-sensitive surgical instruments and plastics?
back:
- Ethylene oxide gas.
- Functions by alkylating proteins and nucleic acids.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which 'Standard Precautions' must the surgical team apply to all patients regardless of infection status?
back:
• Limit contact with biological fluids/mucous membranes.
• Wear gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection for potential splashes.
• Strict hand hygiene after removing gloves.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): 'Standard precautions should be applied to the care of all patients. This includes limiting health care worker contact with all secretions or biological fluids; skin lesions, mucous membranes, and blood or body fluids.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What are the three simplified clinical criteria for diagnosing a Surgical Site Infection (SSI)?
back:
• Any purulent discharge at the site.
• Abscess formation.
• Spreading cellulitis at the site within one month of operation.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): 'Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: List two common surgical practices now 'proven not effective' for preventing SSI.
back:
• Preoperative shaving (increases micro-abrasions).
• Fumigation of the operating environment.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): 'Surgical site infections... Proven not effective: Fumigation, Preoperative shaving.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Why is Chlorhexidine preferred over standard Ethanol for a 'surgical scrub'?
back: Chlorhexidine (a chlorinated phenol) provides persistent antimicrobial activity and protein denaturation, making it more effective for preoperative hand disinfection than simple alcohol.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): 'Chlorhexidine is a chlorinated phenol that is widely used as a hand disinfectant prior to surgery (“surgical scrub”) and in the cleansing of wounds.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How should a surgical team sterilize heat-sensitive instruments like plastics and endoscopes?
back:
• Ethylene oxide gas (for heat-sensitive materials/plastics).
• 2% Glutaraldehyde (for endoscopes and respiratory equipment).
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): 'Surgical instruments that can be damaged by moist heat are usually sterilized by exposure to ethylene oxide gas... [Page 232 (Book Page)] Glutaraldehyde... is used to sterilize... endoscopes.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the primary focus of Crew Resource Management (CRM) training for surgical teams?
back:
• Cognitive skills: Situational awareness and decision-making.
• Interpersonal skills: Teamwork and non-judgmental error cross-checking.
citation: Page 258 (Book Page): 'Team members are trained to cross-check each other’s actions, ofer assistance when needed and address errors in a non-judgemental fashion.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Define 'Coal-face Errors' as described in surgical professional responsibility.
back: Specific preventable errors committed by surgeons during patient care, including diagnostic/management errors, resuscitation failures, and technical/operative mistakes.
citation: Page 264 (Book Page): 'Cuschieri and others have described coal-face errors as those that can potentially be committed by surgeons during the care of their patients and include: diagnostic and management errors; resuscitation errors; prophylaxis errors... technical and operative errors.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What does the 'Duty of Candour' mandate after a surgical HAI occurs?
back: The surgical team must provide 'Open Disclosure': a full, honest explanation to the patient/carer, potential consequences, an apology, and a plan to prevent recurrence.
citation: Page 263 (Book Page): 'Communicating honestly with patients after an adverse event, or open disclosure, includes a full explanation of what happened... In the UK they are explicitly outlined in the General Medical Council’s professional duty of candour.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Contrast Safety-I and Safety-II approaches in a surgical HAI context.
back:
• Safety-I: Identifying and preventing errors after they occur.
• Safety-II: Enhancing resilience and capacity so everyday performance succeeds more often.
citation: Page 260 (Book Page): 'Safety 1 places the emphasis on identifying errors after the event... safety 2 acknowledges that healthcare work is resilient and that everyday performance succeeds much more often than it fails.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What clinical governance role does the surgeon hold in hospital HAI prevention?
back: Acting as a senior team leader to report incidents, provide oversight for clinical audit/benchmarking, and model transparent professional behavior.
citation: Page 264 (Book Page): 'the surgeon as the likely senior team leader will play a key role in reporting and communicating these events with patients and carers, other team members and hospital administration.'

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the most critical individual practice for the surgical team to prevent the transmission of HAIs via direct contact?
back: Hand hygiene (thorough washing with soap and water or alcohol-based disinfectants) before and after patient contact.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough. When hand-washing with soap and water is not sufficient, a suitable alcohol-based disinfectant must be employed.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Explain the mechanism by which moist heat (autoclaving) effectively kills resistant surgical pathogens compared to dry heat.
back: Denaturation of proteins; water aids in disrupting noncovalent bonds (like hydrogen bonds) that hold protein structures together.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [In general, heat kills by denaturing proteins... Moist heat sterilizes at a lower temperature than dry heat, because water aids in the disruption of noncovalent bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds), which hold protein chains together.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Distinguish between the goals of sterilization and disinfection for surgical instruments.
back: Sterilization: Kills all microorganisms including resistant spores. Disinfection: Kills many pathogens but leaves some organisms and spores surviving.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: During the 'Time Out' phase, what must the surgical team confirm immediately before the skin incision?
back: Patient identity, procedure, incision site, and confirmation that antibiotic prophylaxis was given within the last 60 minutes.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): [Before skin incision (with nurse, anaesthetist and surgeon)... Confirm the patient’s name, procedure, and where the incision will be made. Has antibiotic prophylaxis been given within the last 60 minutes?]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the optimal pharmacological timing for the surgical team to administer prophylactic antibiotics to prevent SSI?
back: Within 60 minutes prior to the surgical incision to ensure peak tissue levels during the procedure.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): [Has antibiotic prophylaxis been given within the last 60 minutes? Yes/Not applicable]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: List the three simplified clinical criteria used by the surgical team to recognize a Surgical Site Infection (SSI).
back: 1. Purulent discharge. 2. Abscess formation. 3. Spreading cellulitis at the site within one month of surgery.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How should the surgical team apply Standard Precautions when handling blood or body fluids from any patient?
back: Wear gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection for any contact that may lead to clothes or face contamination.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions should be applied to the care of all patients... Health care workers must wear gloves for each contact which may lead to contamination, and also gown, mask and eye protection if contamination of clothes or the face is anticipated.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: In high-risk environments, how does Crew Resource Management (CRM) help the surgical team mitigate the risk of HAIs?
back: Training members to cross-check each other's aseptic techniques and address errors non-judgementally to maintain situational awareness.
citation: Page 258 (Book Page): [Team members are trained to cross-check each other’s actions, offer assistance when needed and address errors in a non-judgemental fashion. Debriefing and providing feedback are key components of CRM training.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Why is preoperative shaving listed as a 'proven not effective' measure by surgical infection control standards?
back: It creates micro-abrasions that harbor bacteria, increasing SSI risk; if hair removal is necessary, clippers are preferred.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Surgical site infections... Proven not effective: Preoperative shaving.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: State the precise autoclave parameters required to sterilize surgical instruments and kill spores.
back: Steam at 121°C under 15 lb/in² pressure for 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [an autoclave chamber is used in which steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes. This kills even the highly heat-resistant spores.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which three time points define the surgical safety checklist protocol to ensure patient safety?
back: 1. Before induction of anesthesia (Sign In). 2. Before skin incision (Time Out). 3. Before the patient leaves the operating room (Sign Out).
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [The surgical safety checklist identifies specific checks to be carried out at three obligatory time points (Figure 15.1).]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Which intraoperative surgical team interventions are evidence-based for minimizing surgical site infection (SSI) risks?
back: - Timely administration of optimal antibiotic prophylaxis. - Adherence to strict aseptic practices in the OR. - Maintaining a clean operating environment. - Utilizing proper surgical technique and attire.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Table 2: Measures for prevention of infection... Surgical site infections... Proven effective: Surgical technique, Clean operating environment, Staff attire... Optimal antibiotic prophylaxis, Aseptic practice in operating room]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What is the most critical route-based practice for preventing hospital-acquired infection (HAI)?
back: Hand hygiene (hand-washing). This includes using soap and water or alcohol-based disinfectants as per WHO 'Clean Care is Safer Care' guidelines.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough... In the year 2009, WHO developed guidelines for hand hygiene known as 'Clean Care is Safer Care'.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Define the standard physical parameters for sterilization using a healthcare autoclave.
back: Exposure to moist heat (steam) at 121 degrees Celsius under 15 lb/in2 pressure for 15 to 20 minutes to kill spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121 degrees C under a pressure of 15 lb/in2 for 15 minutes.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Differentiate between 'Isolation' and 'Quarantine' as infection control work practices.
back: Isolation: Separates infected/communicable individuals. Quarantine: Limits movement of healthy persons exposed to infection during the incubation period to prevent contact with non-exposed individuals.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page)-127: [Isolation is defined as 'separation... of infected persons'... In contrast to isolation, quarantine applies to restrictions on the healthy contacts of an infectious disease.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Identify the three obligatory time points for the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.
back: 1. Before induction of anesthesia (Sign In). 2. Before skin incision (Time Out). 3. Before the patient leaves the operating room (Sign Out).
citation: Page 241 (Book Page): [The surgical safety checklist identifies specific checks to be carried out at three obligatory time points (Figure 15.1).]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Under Standard Precautions, when is a healthcare worker required to wear gloves?
back: During every contact with blood, biological fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes, skin lesions, or contaminated clinical items.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Health care workers must wear gloves for each contact which may lead to contamination... blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes and contaminated items.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What is the chronological definition used to identify Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)?
back: Pneumonia presenting at least 48 hours after hospital admission that was not present or incubating at the time of entry.
citation: Page 560 (Book Page): [Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined as an episode of pneumonia that presents at least 48 hours after admission to hospital and was not incubating at the time of admission.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Name three 'proven effective' procedural interventions to prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP).
back: 1. Aseptic intubation and suctioning. 2. Limiting the duration of ventilation. 3. Prioritizing non-invasive ventilation (NIV) over invasive methods.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Pneumonia Ventilator-associated: Aseptic intubation and suctioning; Limit duration; Non-invasive ventilation.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which specific immunizations are high-priority for protecting healthcare staff from occupational exposure?
back: Hepatitis B, yearly Influenza, Measles, Mumps, Rubella (MMR), Tetanus, and Diphtheria.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Immunizations recommended for staff include: hepatitis A and B, yearly influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, tetanus, and diphtheria.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Explain why 70 percent ethanol is more effective as a disinfectant than 100 percent ethanol.
back: Maximal biocidal activity for denaturing proteins and disrupting lipid membranes requires the presence of water as a catalyst.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): [Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Enlist three environmental control measures used to suppress the spread of hospital microorganisms.
back: 1. Dust control (wet dusting/vacuuming). 2. Adequate ventilation and lighting. 3. Disinfection of patient excretions (sputum, urine, feces) and laundry.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Dust control: suppression of dust by wet dusting and vacuum cleaning... ensuring adequate lighting and ventilation... patient's urine, faeces, sputum should be properly disinfected.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What are the standard physical parameters for sterilization by autoclaving?
back:
- Temperature: 121°C
- Pressure: 15 lb/in²
- Duration: 15–20 minutes
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in2 for 15 minutes.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which agent is preferred for sterilizing heat-sensitive surgical instruments and plastics?
back:
- Ethylene oxide gas
- Mechanism: Alkylates proteins and nucleic acids
- Use: Heat-sensitive materials
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide gas is used extensively in hospitals for the sterilization of heat-sensitive materials such as surgical instruments and plastics.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which chemical agent is highly effective for sterilizing endoscopes and respiratory equipment?
back:
- Glutaraldehyde
- Features: Two reactive aldehyde groups; 10x more effective than formaldehyde
- Advantage: Lower toxicity
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Glutaraldehyde, which has two reactive aldehyde groups, is 10 times more effective than formaldehyde and is less toxic. In hospitals, it is used to sterilize respiratory therapy equipment, endoscopes, and hemodialysis equipment.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What specific environmental practices prevent the aerosolization of bacteria from hospital dust?
back:
- Wet dusting
- Vacuum cleaning
- Prohibition of dry sweeping or shaking linens
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Suppression of dust by wet dusting and vacuum cleaning are important control measures.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: List three evidence-based practices to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTI).
back:
- Limit catheterization duration
- Use aseptic technique during insertion
- Maintain a strictly closed drainage system
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Urinary tract infections... Proven effective: Limit duration of catheter, Aseptic technique at insertion, Maintain closed drainage.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Enlist three proven preoperative practices for preventing Surgical Site Infections (SSI).
back:
- Preoperative shower and local skin prep
- Optimal antibiotic prophylaxis timing
- Limiting preoperative hospital stay
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Surgical site infections... Proven effective: Limiting preoperative hospital stay, Preoperative shower and local skin preparation of patient, Optimal antibiotic prophylaxis.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: A patient requires a central line. Which practices minimize vascular device infections?
back:
- Surgical asepsis during insertion
- Limitation of dressing change frequency
- Prompt removal if infection is suspected
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Central lines... Surgical asepsis for insertion, Limitation of frequency of dressing change... Removal if infection suspected.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Identify the three obligatory time points for the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.
back:
- Before induction of anaesthesia (Sign In)
- Before skin incision (Time Out)
- Before patient leaves operating room (Sign Out)
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [The surgical safety checklist identifies specific checks to be carried out at three obligatory time points (Figure 15.1).]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: When should alcohol-based disinfectants be utilized instead of standard soap and water?
back:
- When hand-washing with soap/water is insufficient
- For rapid clinical decontamination
- To meet WHO 'Clean Care is Safer Care' standards
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [When hand-washing with soap and water is not sufficient, a suitable alcohol-based disinfectant must be employed for hand-washing.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Why is the prohibition of syringe and needle reuse critical in clinical settings?
back:
- Prevents HIV transmission
- Prevents Hepatitis B and C transmission
- Reduces mortality (estimated 1.3 million annual deaths globally)
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): [Each year, unsafe injections cause 1.3 million deaths, primarily as a result of transmission of hepatitis viruses and human immunodeficiency virus.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which specific clinical conditions mandate the exclusion of healthcare staff from duty to prevent HAI transmission?
back:
Staff must stay away until cured if suffering from:
- Skin diseases
- Sore throat or common cold
- Ear infections
- Diarrhea or dysentery
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Those who are suffering from skin diseases, sore throat, common cold, ear infection, diarrhoea or dysentery and other infectious ailments should be kept away from work until completely cured.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Contrast Barrier Nursing and Task Nursing as safe work practices in infection control.
back:
- Barrier Nursing: Physical isolation of infected patients.
- Task Nursing: Specializing tasks (e.g., specific staff for wound care) to minimize cross-contamination routes.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Nursing techniques: Barrier nursing and task nursing have also been recommended to minimize cross infection.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What is the preferred method for sterilizing heat-sensitive intravenous solutions to ensure they are pyrogen-free?
back:
- Filtration
- Typically uses nitrocellulose filters with a 0.22 μm pore size to retain all bacteria and spores.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [Filtration is the preferred method of sterilizing certain solutions (e.g., those with heat-sensitive components)... solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free prior to autoclaving.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Define the application of the "No-touch technique" in standard infection control precautions.
back: - Clinicians avoid direct hand contact with sterile supplies, wounds, or mucous membranes, regardless of glove use, using instruments instead.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions for all patients are as follows... Use no touch technique wherever possible.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Regarding Surgical Site Infection (SSI) prevention, identify the preoperative practice proven to be ineffective.
back:
- Preoperative shaving
- (Note: Clipping is preferred as shaving causes micro-abrasions that increase infection risk).
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Table 2: Measures for prevention of infection... Surgical site infections... Proven not effective: Preoperative shaving.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: How should healthcare facilities manage dust to reduce the risk of airborne infection transmission?
back:
- Suppression via wet dusting
- Vacuum cleaning
- Avoid dry sweeping or bed-making techniques that release dust particles into the air.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Suppression of dust by wet dusting and vacuum cleaning are important control measures.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What is the immediate standard precaution protocol for clinical biological spills?
back:
- Prompt cleaning of infective material spills
- Immediate hand washing following the removal of gloves used during the cleanup.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Clean up spills of infective material promptly... Wash hands immediately after removing gloves.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Contrast "Tincture of Iodine" and "Iodophors" in preoperative skin disinfection.
back:
- Tincture: Ethanol-based (2%), effective but irritating; must be removed with alcohol.
- Iodophors: Detergent-based complexes (e.g., Povidone-iodine); less irritating and commonly used for surgical prep.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Iodophors are complexes of iodine with detergents that are frequently used to prepare the skin prior to surgery because they are less irritating than tincture of iodine.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which administrative body formulated the safe practices for hospital isolation and disinfection procedures?
back:
- Hospital Control of Infection Committee
- They set policies for admissions, disinfection standards, and compliance monitoring.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [There should be a hospital “Control of Infection Committee” to formulate policies regarding admission of infectious cases, isolation facilities, disinfection procedures...]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: How is the biological efficacy of the autoclaving process verified in a healthcare setting?
back: - Through testing with highly heat-resistant spore-forming organisms (e.g., Clostridium or Geobacillus species).
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [To test the effectiveness of the autoclaving process, spore-forming organisms, such as members of the genus Clostridium, are used.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the most common route of infection transmission that the surgical team must manage?
back:
• The hands.
• Thorough hand-washing with soap or alcohol-based disinfectants is required.
• The surgical team should follow WHO "Clean Care is Safer Care" guidelines.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The most common route of infection is via the hands. When dealing with patients, hand-washing must be thorough. When hand-washing with soap and water is not sufficient, a suitable alcohol-based disinfectant must be employed for hand-washing.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: List three clinical criteria used by the surgical team to identify a Surgical Site Infection (SSI).
back:
• Any purulent discharge at the site.
• Abscess formation.
• Spreading cellulitis occurring within one month post-operation.
citation: Page 366 (Book Page): [Surgical site infection: Any purulent discharge, abscess, or spreading cellulitis at the surgical site during the month after the operation.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Within what specific timeframe must the surgical team administer antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent SSIs?
back: • Within the last 60 minutes prior to the skin incision.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): [Has antibiotic prophylaxis been given within the last 60 minutes? (Before skin incision section)]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Why is limiting the preoperative hospital stay a critical surgical team role in preventing HAIs?
back:
• It is a proven effective measure to prevent SSIs.
• It reduces patient exposure to hospital pathogens and subsequent colonization risk.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Surgical site infections... Proven effective: Limiting preoperative hospital stay]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: True/False: Fumigation of the operating room is an evidence-based intervention for the prevention of SSIs.
back:
• False.
• Fumigation is proven not effective for preventing surgical site infections.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Surgical site infections... Proven not effective: Fumigation]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: What is the mandatory protocol for surgical team members suffering from a common cold or skin disease?
back:
• They must be kept away from work until completely cured.
• This prevents potential transmission of infectious agents to susceptible patients.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Those who are suffering from skin diseases, sore throat, common cold... should be kept away from work until completely cured.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: In the operating theater, when must the team use gloves as part of Standard Precautions?
back:
• During every contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions.
• When contact with mucous membranes or contaminated items is anticipated.
• Hands must be washed immediately after removing gloves.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions for all patients are as follows: Wear gloves when in contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes and contaminated items. Wash hands immediately after removing gloves.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: Identify the three obligatory time points for the surgical team to perform the WHO Safety Checklist.
back:
• 1. Before induction of anaesthesia.
• 2. Before skin incision.
• 3. Before the patient leaves the operating room.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): [Surgical Safety Checklist: Before induction of anaesthesia; Before skin incision; Before patient leaves operating room]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: A surgeon is disposing of a used scalpel. What are the two core safety roles regarding sharps?
back:
• Handle all sharps with extreme care to prevent occupational exposure.
• Utilize "no touch" techniques wherever possible to minimize needle-stick or blade injuries.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [All sharps should be handled with extreme care. Use no touch technique wherever possible.]

category: Outline the role of the surgical team in preventing HAIs
front: Q: How must the surgical environment be managed to control bacteria-laden hospital dust?
back:
• Use wet dusting and vacuum cleaning to suppress particles.
• Avoid dry sweeping/dusting, which releases bacteria and viruses into the air.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Hospital dust contains numerous bacteria and viruses. The dust is released during sweeping, dusting and bed making. Suppression of dust by wet dusting and vacuum cleaning are important control measures.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: List the four fundamental Standard (Routine) Precautions applicable to all healthcare patients.
back:
- Prompt hand hygiene after contact.
- PPE (gloves/masks) for fluid/blood exposure.
- Extreme care during sharps handling.
- Immediate cleaning of infective spills.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions for all patients are as follows: — Wash hands promptly after contact with infective material. — Wear gloves when in contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions... — All sharps should be handled with extreme care. — Clean up spills of infective material promptly.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Identify the three primary 'proven effective' work practices for preventing nosocomial vascular device infections.
back:
- Strict aseptic technique during insertion.
- Maintaining a closed infusion/drainage system.
- Limiting the duration of catheterization (early removal).
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [Vascular device Infections... Proven effective: Aseptic technique at insertion; Maintain closed system; Limit duration; Local skin preparation.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What are the two primary methods of hand hygiene recommended to break the 'hands' route of transmission?
back:
• Hand-washing with soap and water (standard mechanical removal).
• Alcohol-based disinfectants (employed when hand-washing is insufficient or hands are not visibly soiled).
• Thoroughness is critical for all patient contacts.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [When hand-washing with soap and water is not sufficient, a suitable alcohol-based disinfectant must be employed for hand-washing. In the year 2009, WHO developed guidelines for hand hygiene known as “Clean Care is Safer Care”.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Define the mandatory application and core components of 'Standard Precautions' in a healthcare setting.
back:
• Application: Applied to all patients regardless of diagnosis.
• Exposure limits: Contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes.
• Gear: Gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection based on anticipated exposure.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Standard precautions should be applied to the care of all patients. This includes limiting health care worker contact with all secretions or biological fluids; skin lesions, mucous membranes, and blood or body fluids. Health care workers must wear gloves for each contact which may lead to contamination, and also gown, mask and eye protection.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Identify two specific environmental practices used to suppress pathogen-laden dust in hospital wards.
back:
• Wet dusting: Prevents aerosolization of bacteria and viruses.
• Vacuum cleaning: Preferred over dry sweeping to prevent releasing particles into the air.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The dust is released during sweeping, dusting and bed making. Suppression of dust by wet dusting and vacuum cleaning are important control measures.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: A surgeon is preparing for a procedure. Identify the three obligatory time points for the Surgical Safety Checklist.
back:
• Before induction of anaesthesia (Sign In).
• Before skin incision (Time Out).
• Before patient leaves operating room (Sign Out).
• Goal: Reduces perioperative mortality and major complications.
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [The surgical safety checklist identifes specifc checks to be carried out at three obligatory time points... Before induction of anaesthesia... Before skin incision... Before patient leaves operating room.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Contrast the efficacy of 'Sterilization' versus 'Disinfection' regarding the elimination of bacterial spores.
back:
• Sterilization: Complete killing/removal of all life forms, including highly resistant bacterial spores.
• Disinfection: Kills many pathogens but not all; spores typically survive the process.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms. For adequate disinfection, pathogens must be killed, but some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What is the recommended safe practice for the disposal and handling of medical sharps?
back:
• Extreme care during handling; use 'no touch' techniques where possible.
• Immediate disposal in puncture-resistant containers.
• Avoid recapping needles to prevent occupational exposure.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [All sharps should be handled with extreme care. Clean up spills of infective material promptly... Use no touch technique wherever possible.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Enlist four environmental and nursing measures specifically designed to control droplet-borne infection transmission.
back:
• Use of face masks.
• Proper bed spacing to prevent overcrowding.
• Ensuring adequate ward lighting and ventilation.
• Implementation of barrier nursing techniques.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [(f) Control of droplet infection : Use of face masks, proper bed spacing, prevention of overcrowding and ensuring adequate lighting and ventilation are important control measures. (g) Nursing techniques : Barrier nursing and task nursing have also been recommended.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Define the four main types of isolation used based on patient risk and pathogen severity.
back:
1. Standard isolation.
2. Strict isolation (for highly dangerous pathogens).
3. Protective isolation (for immunocompromised patients).
4. High security isolation (for extreme biohazards).
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [The type of isolation varies with the mode of spread and severity of the disease. There are several types of isolation — standard isolation, strict isolation, protective isolation, high security isolation (136).]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which immunizations are mandatory for healthcare staff to prevent occupational and nosocomial transmission?
back:
• Hepatitis B and Hepatitis A.
• Yearly Influenza.
• MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella).
• Tetanus and Diphtheria.
• BCG/Mantoux test for Tuberculosis baseline.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Immunizations recommended for staff include: hepatitis A and B, yearly influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, tetanus, and diphtheria. Immunization against varicella may be considered in specific cases. The Mantoux skin test will document a previous tuberculosis infection.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Specify the standard parameters (temp/pressure/time) for effective moist heat sterilization in an autoclave.
back:
• Temperature: 121°C.
• Pressure: 15 lb/in².
• Time: 15–20 minutes.
• Purpose: Denatures proteins and kills heat-resistant spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is usually carried out by autoclaving, which consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in² for 15 minutes.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: How should medical equipment contaminated with infective material be managed between patient uses?
back: Items must be either discarded, disinfected, or sterilized.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): Ensure that patient-care equipment, supplies and linen contaminated with infective material is either discarded, or disinfected or sterilized between each patient use.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: What is the recommended alternative for disinfecting soiled linen when a washing machine is unavailable?
back: The soiled linen can be boiled to ensure pathogen destruction.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): If no washing machine is available for linen soiled with infective material, the linen can be boiled.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Which three specific patient excretions require proper disinfection as part of hospital waste control?
back:
1. Urine
2. Faeces
3. Sputum
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): the articles used by the patient as well as patient's urine, faeces, sputum should be properly disinfected.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: What is the immediate protocol for an accidental spill of infective material in a healthcare setting?
back: Clean up the spill promptly to minimize environmental contamination.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): Clean up spills of infective material promptly.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: What mandatory hand hygiene step is required immediately after removing clinical gloves?
back: Wash hands immediately after glove removal.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): Wash hands immediately after removing gloves.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: What procedural technique is recommended to avoid direct handling of contaminated materials?
back: Employ a 'no touch technique' whenever possible.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): Use no touch technique wherever possible.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: State the standard precaution regarding the physical handling of medical sharps.
back: All sharps must be handled with extreme care.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): All sharps should be handled with extreme care.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
coreConcept: Public Health Impact of Sharps Mismanagement
front: In resource-poor settings, what are the primary fatal consequences of unsafe sharps management and reuse?
back: Transmission of blood-borne pathogens, specifically HIV and Hepatitis viruses.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): unsafe injections cause 1.3 million deaths, primarily as a result of transmission of hepatitis viruses and human immunodeficiency virus.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: What must be done with patient articles to maintain environmental infection control?
back: Properly disinfect all articles used by the patient.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): The articles used by the patient as well as patient's urine, faeces, sputum should be properly disinfected.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: When standard hand-washing is insufficient for decontamination, what specific agent should be used?
back: A suitable alcohol-based disinfectant.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): When hand-washing with soap and water is not sufficient, a suitable alcohol-based disinfectant must be employed for hand-washing.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: What is the primary safety requirement for handling needles and sharps under standard hospital precautions?
back: Sharps must be handled with extreme care. Key protocols include: 1. Avoiding recapping needles. 2. Immediate disposal in puncture-resistant containers. 3. Ensuring appropriate waste handling to prevent occupational exposure.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): All sharps should be handled with extreme care. Ensure appropriate waste handling.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
coreConcept: Public Health Impact of Syringe Reuse
front: Q: Identify the specific viral pathogens and mortality impact associated with the unsafe disposal and reuse of medical syringes.
back: Unsafe disposal/reuse causes ~1.3 million annual deaths. Primary pathogens transmitted include: 1. Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). 2. Hepatitis B virus. 3. Hepatitis C virus.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): Each year, unsafe injections cause 1.3 million deaths, primarily as a result of transmission of hepatitis viruses and human immunodeficiency virus.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: What is the mandatory protocol for handling medical sharps according to standard precautions?
back:
* All sharps must be handled with extreme care
* Use "no-touch" techniques whenever possible
* Never reuse needles or syringes without sterilization.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [All sharps should be handled with extreme care. ... Use no touch technique wherever possible.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: Identify the major disease transmission risks associated with unsafe injection and disposal practices.
back:
* Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)
* Hepatitis C Virus (HCV)
* Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
citation: Page 128 (Book Page): [Each year, unsafe injections cause 1.3 million deaths, primarily as a result of transmission of hepatitis viruses and human immunodeficiency virus.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: What is the immediate required action for spills of infective material in a healthcare setting?
back: Clean up spills of infective material promptly to prevent environmental contamination and transmission.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Clean up spills of infective material promptly.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: How should contaminated patient-care equipment be managed between use on different patients?
back:
* Discard (single-use items)
* Disinfect (low-risk items)
* Sterilize (high-risk items).
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Ensure that patient-care equipment, supplies and linen contaminated with infective material is either discarded, or disinfected or sterilized between each patient use.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: List the specific patient excretions that require proper disinfection to prevent nosocomial spread.
back:
* Urine
* Faeces
* Sputum.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [The articles used by the patient as well as patient's urine, faeces, sputum should be properly disinfected.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: What specific hand hygiene step is required after disposing of contaminated gloves?
back: Wash hands immediately after removing gloves to eliminate potential microbial seepage or contamination.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Wash hands immediately after removing gloves.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: In an AEFI investigation, which waste-related items are tested for sterility?
back:
* Needles
* Syringes
* Suspect vaccines and diluents.
citation: Page 124 (Book Page): [the needles and syringe for sterility. Testing should be requested on a clear suspicion and not as a routine.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: Why is filtration preferred over autoclaving for certain intravenous solutions?
back:
* Removes heat-sensitive components
* Ensures solutions are pyrogen-free (removes heat-resistant endotoxins from dead bacteria).
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): [solutions are now filtered to make them pyrogen-free prior to autoclaving. ... The most commonly used filter ... has a pore size of 0.22 μm. This size will retain all bacteria and spores.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: How should heat-sensitive surgical instruments be sterilized if moist heat is damaging?
back: Use exposure to Ethylene Oxide gas for sterilization.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Surgical instruments that can be damaged by moist heat are usually sterilized by exposure to ethylene oxide gas.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: What are the standard parameters for autoclaving to ensure the destruction of bacterial spores?
back:
* Temperature: 121°C
* Pressure: 15 lb/in²
* Duration: 15–20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in2, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes. This kills even the highly heat-resistant spores.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What are the two most critical hand hygiene timings required under standard precautions?
back: Hand hygiene must be performed promptly after contact with any infective material and immediately after the removal of gloves.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Wash hands promptly after contact with infective material. ...Wash hands immediately after removing gloves.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: How do gowns and masks function as safe work practices in infection control?
back: Gowns prevent the contamination of the healthcare worker's clothing, while masks protect the face and mucous membranes from splashes or droplets.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [gown: should be of washable material ...mask : surgical masks made of cloth or paper may be used to protect from splashes.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Distinguish between the outcomes of sterilization and disinfection in a healthcare setting.
back: Sterilization removes all microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores; disinfection kills most pathogens but may spare certain organisms and spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores ...Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all, microorganisms.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: A healthcare worker encounters a large blood spill. What are the standardized safe handling steps?
back: Wear protective gloves immediately, clean up the spill promptly, and ensure all contaminated material is discarded through appropriate waste handling channels.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [Clean up spills of infective material promptly. ...Ensure appropriate waste handling.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What is the primary biochemical mechanism of action for chlorine-based hospital disinfectants?
back: Chlorine acts as an oxidant that cross-links essential sulfhydryl groups in microbial enzymes, forming inactive disulfides to kill the pathogen.
citation: Page 231 (Book Page): [Chlorine is a powerful oxidizing agent that kills by cross-linking essential sulfhydryl groups in enzymes to form the inactive disulfide.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Which baseline screening test is mandatory for hospital staff to monitor occupational tuberculosis exposure?
back: The Mantoux skin test is required at recruitment to document previous infection and establish a baseline for health surveillance.
citation: Page 368 (Book Page): [The Mantoux skin test will document a previous tuberculosis infection and must be obtained as a base-line.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: How does the Surgical Safety Checklist apply to reduce perioperative infection and mortality?
back: It mandates standardized checks, including antibiotic prophylaxis and instrument counts, at three obligatory time points: pre-induction, pre-incision, and before leaving the theatre.
citation: Page 261 (Book Page): [The surgical safety checklist identifies specific checks to be carried out at three obligatory time points ...associated with a reduction in perioperative mortality.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: A patient presents with a cough and purulent sputum. When should isolation be discontinued?
back: Isolation should persist for the specific period of communicability; for infectious tuberculosis, this typically requires three weeks of effective chemotherapy.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [Isolation is defined as “separation, for the period of communicability ...The duration of isolation is determined by the duration of communicability.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: What safe work practices are required when handling medical sharps in healthcare settings?
back: Sharps must be handled with extreme care, using no-touch techniques where possible, and disposed of in puncture-resistant containers without recapping needles.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): [All sharps should be handled with extreme care. ...Use no touch technique wherever possible.]

category: Discuss the safe work practices that reduce the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings
front: Q: Specify the exact physical parameters required for effective autoclaving of surgical instruments.
back: Instruments must be exposed to moist heat (steam) at 121°C under 15 lb/in² pressure for 15 to 20 minutes.
citation: Page 233 (Book Page): [steam, at a pressure of 15 lb/in, reaches a temperature of 121°C and is held at that temperature for 15 to 20 minutes.]

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: What are the standard physical parameters for autoclaving medical waste and instruments?
back:
• Temperature: 121°C.
• Pressure: 15 lb/in².
• Duration: 15–20 minutes.
• Purpose: Kills all microorganisms and highly resistant bacterial spores.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): [autoclaving] consists of exposure to steam at 121°C under a pressure of 15 lb/in2 for 15 minutes.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: How does ethylene oxide gas chemically achieve sterilization for heat-sensitive clinical materials?
back:
• Mechanism: Alkylation.
• Targets: Essential amino and hydroxyl groups in both proteins and nucleic acids.
• Use: For plastics and instruments damaged by moist heat.
citation: Page 232 (Book Page): [Ethylene oxide] kills by alkylating both proteins and nucleic acids.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: How do sterilization and disinfection differ regarding the survival of bacterial spores?
back:
• Sterilization: Removes all life forms, including resistant bacterial spores.
• Disinfection: Kills pathogens but allows some organisms and spores to survive.
• Context: Autoclaving vs. chemical disinfectants.
citation: Page 228 (Book Page): Sterilization is the killing or removal of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores... Disinfection is the killing of many, but not all... some organisms and bacterial spores may survive.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: In standard precautions, which specific instruction applies to the handling of all medical sharps?
back:
• Instruction: Handle with extreme care.
• Procedure: Use 'no-touch' techniques whenever possible.
• Goal: Prevent occupational exposure and cross-infection.
citation: Page 367 (Book Page): All sharps should be handled with extreme care... Use no touch technique wherever possible.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: Why is 70% ethanol more effective than 100% ethanol for clinical skin antisepsis?
back:
• Requirement: Presence of water.
• Mechanism: Water is needed for maximal protein denaturation and membrane disorganization.
• Clinical use: Skin cleaning before immunization.
citation: Page 230 (Book Page): Ethanol requires the presence of water for maximal activity (i.e., it is far more effective at 70% than at 100%).

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: Which method is preferred for sterilizing heat-sensitive intravenous solutions to remove endotoxins and bacteria?
back:
• Method: Filtration.
• Material: Nitrocellulose filter.
• Pore size: 0.22 μm.
• Benefit: Renders solutions pyrogen-free.
citation: Page 234 (Book Page): The most commonly used filter is composed of nitrocellulose and has a pore size of 0.22 μm. This size will retain all bacteria and spores.

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: During clinical service assessment, which specific activities must be observed regarding used vaccine vials?
back:
• Observation: Disposal of opened vials.
• Safety checks: Reconstitution technique and needle/syringe safety.
• Risk management: Identifying contaminated open vials.
citation: Page 124 (Book Page): [Observe] Immunization procedures (reconstitution, drawing up vaccine, injection technique, safety of needles and syringes; disposal of opened vials).

category: Describe the safe disposal of sharps and waste
front: Q: Reusing syringes without sterilization contributes to the transmission of which three major viral pathogens?
back:
• Pathogens: Hepatitis B virus (HBV), Hepatitis C virus (HCV), and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
• Impact: Causes approximately 1.3 million deaths annually worldwide.
citation: Page 262 (Book Page): unsafe injections cause 1.3 million deaths, primarily as a result of transmission of hepatitis viruses and human immunodeficiency virus.
